Place, local memory & heritage · Photographic essay

Modern Salamis and the Memory of Darius’ Ghost

How the ancient naval battle is remembered, performed and reinterpreted in the everyday landscape of contemporary Salamis.

Antonis ChaliakopoulosPhD candidate in Classical Archaeology, University of AthensSalamis, Greece · 2024–2026
ExploreIntroduction01 · Kynosoura02 · Aeschylus03 · The trireme04 · Performing the past05 · The liquid tombSources & credits
INTRODUCTION

The past in the present

In 480 BCE, at the Battle of Salamis, the allied Greek fleet defeated the invading Persian forces. More than 2,500 years later, the naval battle retains a prominent place in the collective imagination of the local population.

Today, on the island of Salamis, this classical past is remembered and actively performed as an essential pillar of local identity.

Through an annual festival known as the Salaminia, the island transforms into a theatrical stage on which history—much like the spirit of King Darius in Aeschylus’s tragedy The Persians—is brought back to life and reinterpreted in a contemporary context. The classical past is ever-present in symbols, particularly the trireme; in performances such as the Salaminia; and in monuments such as the so-called Tomb of the Salamis Fighters.

This photographic essay examines Salamis as a lieu de mémoire (a site of memory), described by Pierre Nora (1989) as a site “where memory crystallizes and secretes.” It explores the tension between the idealised, distant classical past of the island’s ancestors and contemporary Salamis.

01 / A HEROIC LANDSCAPE

The Heroes of Kynosoura

The Kynosoura peninsula in eastern Salamis has been connected with the naval battle since antiquity as the location where the victors erected a battle monument, or tropaion.

In modern times, Kynosoura became central to the battle’s memory because of the discovery and symbolism associated with the so-called “Tomb of the Salamis Fighters.” In 2006, the municipality installed a bronze sculpture by Achilleas Vasileiou that greets visitors arriving at the site.

The sculpture depicts two nude warriors striding forward on the prow of a trireme: one wields a bow, while the other prepares to hurl a spear. The monument embodies an idealised heroic memory of the battle and has become a ubiquitous local symbol (Chairetakis 2024).

The ancient site and its modern sculpture also stand within a long-running political and legal dispute over the ownership and status of Kynosoura. Its cultural landscape has been affected by the expansion of the shipyard industry since the 1960s and by an unregulated rubbish dump that occupied the peninsula’s tip until recently (Belavilas and Prentou 2018).

02 / WORDS IN STONE

Aeschylus in the Weeds

Further along the coast, at Akti Themistokleous—named after the Athenian general who played a major role in the Battle of Salamis—lies another modern monument devoted to the memory of the battle, close to Ampelaki, the site of the ancient city’s harbour.

A stone stele carries the paean from Aeschylus’s Persians, in G. M. Cookson’s translation:

Forth, sons of Hellas! free your land, and free Your children and your wives, the native seats Of Gods your fathers worshipped and their graves. This is a bout that hazards all ye have.

Aeschylus, Persians, translated by G. M. Cookson

The stele is flanked by round shields representing the allied Greek city-states that fought in 480 BCE. The monument connects the landscape with the ancient battle while also functioning as a tool of cultural diplomacy, creating historical bonds among the modern municipalities represented by the flags.

The installation is juxtaposed with the industrial infrastructure of Perama and, across the water, the container-port cranes associated with COSCO.

03 / THE IMAGE OF A WARSHIP

The Trireme

The memory of Salamis is inseparable from the trireme, a vessel that has become a brand symbol for the island. It serves as the official emblem of the Municipality of Salamis and appears in many other settings.

Walking through Ampelaki, where the allied Greek fleet once departed to face the Persian forces, one encounters the buildings of Salamis Shipyards, identified by a blue sign bearing the image of a trireme.

The ancient warship thus lends historical depth both to the municipality and to the promotion of a modern industry. As the next section shows, a reconstructed trireme is also used during the Salaminia commemorations.

04 / CEREMONY & IDENTITY

Performing the Past

This relationship with the past reaches a climax during the modern Salaminia commemorations in late September. The Hellenic Navy’s reconstructed trireme Olympias is towed into the harbour at Kamatero, where naval personnel stand in formation in anticipation of the festivities.

During the ceremony, a theatrical adaptation of Aeschylus’s Persians—the oldest surviving Greek tragedy and a rare tragedy centred on an identifiable historical event—is typically staged. Political speeches frame the relationship between Salamis, the classical past, the modern Greek state and the West.

The commemoration brings together members of the clergy, representatives of the Hellenic Navy—which regards the fleet that fought at Salamis as its distant predecessor—and politicians from local, regional and national government.

05 / WATER & MEMORY

The Liquid Tomb

In the national narrative, and in its local version, the sea surrounding Salamis is often referred to reverently as the “liquid tomb” of the ancestors.

Here, it is difficult to say whether memory influences the way we experience the sea, or whether the sea shapes memory in return.

Memory takes the shape of the landscape, and the landscape takes the shape of memory. The sea is fluid and ever-changing: serene one day, angry the next. There is an almost mystical dimension to this identification, in which the national gaze and its object of desire—the landscape, to borrow a term from psychoanalysis—seem to merge.

The sea, an integral part of life on the island, becomes a physical manifestation of a past that haunts Salamis with the burden of proving itself worthy of its ancestors.

Curatorial note

The images in this essay show the island in the present, not the naval battle of 480 BCE. They document how historical memory is expressed through monuments, commercial emblems, public ceremonies and an industrial maritime landscape. The essay’s interpretation is that of its author; the photographs are contemporary sources for the reception of the classical past.
